message:
I run deliveries for a small furniture restorer and I've got a few things to sort for tomorrow.

Can you suggest a name for our new delivery van (staff vote, nothing rude)?

Tomorrow the van can't leave the depot before 08:30 and must be back by 12:00. Three drops, each takes 15 minutes to unload. Drop A has a delivery window of 09:00 to 10:00. Drop B is a shop that needs its delivery done before it opens at 09:30. Drop C is an office that won't accept anything before 11:00. Driving times: depot to A 30 min, depot to B 20 min, depot to C 45 min, A to B 25 min, A to C 40 min, B to C 50 min. The driver also needs a 30-minute break somewhere before 12:00. What order should he go in, and what's the timeline?

Could you also rewrite our delivery text so it sounds friendlier than "Driver arriving. Be in."? List three things the driver should check on furniture before handing it over. Should we give customers a paper delivery note or an emailed one? And define "proof of delivery" in a line for our new part-timer. One more thing: we're thinking of texting customers the evening before with a rough arrival time. Could you draft that evening-before text too, keeping it under 160 characters so it goes as a single message?
response:
## Van name ideas
- **Chester**, after the Chesterfield sofa
- **The Dovetail**
- **Sir Veneer**
- **Mahogany Mo**
- **Old Faithful**, a nod to the restoration trade

## Tomorrow's route: **B → A → C** is the only order that works

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 08:30 | Leave depot |
| 08:50 | Arrive at **B** |
| 08:50–09:05 | Unload at B (done well before the 09:30 opening) |
| 09:05–09:30 | Drive B → A |
| 09:30–09:45 | Unload at **A** (inside the 09:00–10:00 window) |
| 09:45–10:25 | Drive A → C |
| 10:25–10:55 | **30-minute break**, parked near C |
| 10:55–11:00 | Wait for C to open to deliveries |
| 11:00–11:15 | Unload at **C** |
| 11:15–12:00 | Drive C → depot, **back at 12:00** |

**Why other orders fail:**
- Any route that doesn't start at B misses B's 09:30 deadline. For example, going to A first finishes at 09:15, and B would then take until 09:40.
- After B, going to C first would leave A's window long closed by the time the driver got back to it.

**The catch: there's no slack on the return.** C can't start unloading before 11:00, so 11:00 + 15 minutes unloading + 45 minutes driving brings him back at exactly 12:00. Any delay at C, or traffic on the way back, makes him late. Before tomorrow:
- **Ask the office at C** whether they can be ready to receive at 11:00 sharp.
- **Check whether the 12:00 return can flex** by a few minutes if needed.

The wait at C is a natural spot for the break. He could also take it at A from 09:45 to 10:15, and the timeline still finishes at 12:00.

## Friendlier "on the way" text
> Hi [Name], good news: your furniture is on its way! [Driver] should be with you in about [30] minutes. Any problems, just call [number]. Thanks!

## Three checks before handover
1. **Condition.** Check for scratches, dents or marks to the finish, especially any that weren't there when it left the workshop. Point out the restored areas to the customer.
2. **Completeness.** Make sure all parts are present: legs, shelves, keys, handles, glass, cushions and any loose hardware.
3. **Function and stability.** Check that it stands level without rocking, that drawers and doors open and close smoothly, and that locks work.

## Paper or emailed delivery note?
**Default to email.** Have the customer sign on the driver's phone and send the note automatically: it's quicker, can't be lost, and gives you a timestamped record. Keep a few paper copies in the van for customers who'd rather have one or don't use email.

## Proof of delivery, for the part-timer
**Proof of delivery is a signed and dated record, ideally with a photo, showing that the customer received the item in good condition.**

## Evening-before text (well under 160 characters)
> Hi [Name], your furniture from [Business] arrives tomorrow between [9 and 10am]. Questions? Call [number]. Thanks!

With a typical name, a short business name and a phone number filled in, this comes to about 120 characters, so there's room to spare.

**One tip:** avoid emoji and "smart" curly apostrophes or quotes. Either one switches the message to a different encoding, where the single-message limit drops to 70 characters and it may be split and charged as two texts.
